articles.title: Ukraine deals major blow to Putin’s Crimea lifeline, European intel assessment claims
articles.summary:
Ukraine's repeated attacks on the Kerch Bridge, one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's most prized infrastructure projects, have dealt a potentially significant blow to Moscow's military supply routes into occupied Crimea, raising questions about Russia's ability to sustain operations as both sides prepare for a difficult winter.

A European intelligence assessment dated Nov. 18 and obtained by Fox News Digital describes Ukraine's latest assault as likely its most successful attack on the heavily defended crossing, following a coordinated campaign targeting Russian air defenses, radar and electronic warfare systems.

Ret. Gen. Philip Breedlove, former NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe, told Fox News Digital the consequences could extend far beyond the destruction of a symbolic Russian landmark. "The Russians are extremely limited in how they get supplies to Crimea and cutting the Kerch bridge will severely, severely damage their ability to resupply Crimea," Breedlove said.

UKRAINE HITS PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE IN RECORD DRONE BLITZ AS KREMLIN TELLS LAWMAKERS TO PREPARE FOR 'VICTORY'

On Nov. 17, Ukrainian missiles and drones struck the 12-mile bridge linking Russia's Krasnodar region to Crimea, collapsing a major section of the roadway into the Kerch Strait and damaging the adjacent railway.

The crossing, inaugurated by Putin in 2018, has served as both a critical transportation link and a symbol of Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014.

According to the European intelligence assessment, the attack followed a multiweek Ukrainian operation against Russian defensive systems, intended to weaken the bridge's protection before the main strike.

Ukraine subsequently struck the railway again on Nov.19, temporarily halting train traffic and bringing the number of attacks to three in four days.

The damage has disrupted one of Russia's most direct supply connections to Crimea, which Moscow uses to support military operations in southern Ukraine.

PUTIN LAUNCHES UKRAINE BARRAGE HOURS AFTER TRUMP MEETING AMID ALLEGED RUSSIAN MISSILE BREACH OF NATO AIRSPACE

Russia has developed an alternative land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, but the European intelligence assessment warns that shifting additional military supplies onto those roads could create significant vulnerabilities.

The assessment identifies slower transportation routes, exposure to Ukrainian drone attacks and pressure on other logistical infrastructure as potential consequences.

Breedlove said Ukraine's campaign should be viewed as an attempt to weaken Russia's hold on the peninsula, rather than simply destroy a bridge. He argued that Russia's options are further constrained by Ukraine's success in challenging Russian naval power in the northern Black Sea.

He pointed out that Ukraine has used maritime and aerial drones to push back Russia's Black Sea Fleet despite lacking large conventional warships.

The European assessment also warns that repairing the bridge could take months. Although limited road traffic might resume within weeks, replacing the collapsed section could take considerably longer, particularly if Ukrainian attacks continue.

Damage above the Kerch–Yenikale Canal could also disrupt shipping between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS

Despite Ukraine's success in striking the bridge, a European intelligence source familiar with Russian strategic assessments offered a pessimistic view of the broader conflict.

"It has more symbolic meaning, but also logistics is paralyzed right now," the source told Fox News Digital, describing the immediate impact of the attacks.

However, the source warned that Moscow is preparing to intensify its winter offensive while using negotiations with Washington to increase political pressure on Kyiv.

"The general trend is not good for Ukraine," the source said.

According to the source, Russia believes it can sustain military pressure long enough to force Ukraine into territorial concessions, particularly in the east.

"They are very convinced that by spring Ukrainians will give up," the source said, describing Moscow's expectations.

Breedlove strongly disputed the assessment that Russia was gaining the upper hand militarily.

"Militarily, the tide is turning against Russia," Breedlove told Fox News Digital, arguing that Russian forces have suffered staggering casualties while making limited battlefield gains.

He said Russian losses in recent months had been extraordinarily high and argued that Moscow's military was failing to achieve significant territorial advances.

Breedlove did, however, acknowledge a distinction between military momentum and the political pressure facing Ukraine.

He suggested that changes in Washington's approach to negotiations could strengthen Putin's position even if Russian forces were struggling on the battlefield.

The competing assessments highlight a central question facing Ukraine: whether its military successes can translate into greater diplomatic leverage before Russia's winter offensive intensifies.

UKRAINE STRIKES 'ONE OF THE LARGEST OIL REFINERIES' IN SOUTHERN RUSSIA AHEAD OF PUTIN-TRUMP MEETING IN CHINA

Putin has threatened retaliation over the bridge attacks, and on Friday Russia launched a massive missile and drone assault against Ukrainian cities, killing at least eight people, according to Ukrainian authorities.

The strikes came hours after Putin appeared alongside President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a summit in China, as Washington continued efforts to advance peace negotiations.

The European intelligence assessment warns that further Ukrainian attacks on the Kerch Bridge during repairs are highly likely, potentially prolonging disruptions to Russian supplies.

For Moscow, restoring the crossing is now both a logistical challenge and a political priority. For Kyiv, keeping it vulnerable offers a way to increase the cost of Russia's occupation while demonstrating that even Putin's most heavily defended infrastructure remains within reach.

articles.title: New drug combo shrinks tumors in most patients facing aggressive cancer type
articles.summary:
Pairing an experimental pill with standard chemotherapy shrank tumors or halted growth in most patients with advanced pancreatic cancer, according to early clinical trial results presented Friday at a major international cancer conference.

The findings, shared at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium in Barcelona, come from a phase ½ trial testing a daily oral medication called daraxonrasib, along with two standard intravenous chemotherapy drugs, gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel.

The trial focused on 61 patients whose pancreatic cancer had already spread to other organs and who had not yet received treatment for their advanced disease.

PANCREATIC CANCER PATIENT BEN SASSE SEES 'MASSIVE' TUMOR REDUCTION WITH EXPERIMENTAL NEW DRUG

Pancreatic cancer is notoriously difficult to treat because more than half of patients are diagnosed after the disease has already spread, research shows.

In major clinical trials for metastatic pancreatic cancer, chemotherapy alone shrinks tumors in about 23% to 42% of patients, but the disease typically begins growing again after five to six months, and most patients survive between 8 and 11 months.

According to National Cancer Institute data, only about 3% of patients with distant-stage disease live five years past diagnosis.

In the new study, which tracked patients for a median follow-up of 18 months, tumors shrank in 60.7% of cases, including 8.2% where they disappeared entirely on scans. Overall, the combination stopped tumor growth in 90.2% of participants.

FDA APPROVES ONCE-DAILY PILL FOR DEADLY CANCER AFTER PATIENTS' SURVIVAL RATES NEARLY DOUBLE

Patients went a median of 12.8 months before their cancer worsened, almost double the timeframe typically seen with standard chemotherapy, and 76.6% were still alive at the one-year mark, the study found.

"We are now seeing not only substantial tumor shrinkages, including complete responses, but also durable disease control, with median progression-free survival exceeding one year," study lead Dr. Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, said in a press release.

More than 90% of pancreatic cancers are driven by a faulty gene called RAS, which allows tumors to keep growing. Daraxonrasib is designed to turn off that growth signal, something scientists long thought was impossible to fix with medication.

Dr. Elena Garralda, chair of the symposium and co-director of the clinical research program at the Vall d’Hebron Institute of Oncology in Spain, who was not involved in the research, said the results show that RAS-targeted drugs can be combined with existing treatments at the start of treatment to potentially achieve longer-lasting benefits.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Side effects included rash, diarrhea, fatigue and low blood cell counts linked to chemotherapy, most of which were manageable with standard care.

Only 5% of patients stopped treatment because of side effects tied to daraxonrasib.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Researchers emphasized that the findings carry some limitations.

Because this was an early-phase, single-group study involving 61 people, all participants received the experimental combination. Without a direct comparison group of patients receiving standard chemotherapy alone, doctors cannot yet confirm how much better the new regimen performs or whether it definitively extends overall survival.

The findings also apply strictly to metastatic pancreatic cancer, even though RAS mutations drive several other cancers, including certain lung, colorectal and gynecological cancers. Separate studies would be needed to test whether the combination works in those diseases.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

The trial was funded by Revolution Medicines, the California-based developer of daraxonrasib.

To determine whether these early findings translate into a durable survival benefit, researchers have launched a larger, randomized Phase 3 trial, called RASolute-303, which directly compares daraxonrasib — both on its own and combined with chemotherapy — against standard chemotherapy alone.

articles.title: Uber Parking could save you from circling the block
articles.summary:
You finally make it downtown for dinner, but now comes the real challenge. Finding somewhere to park. You circle the block once, then again. Before you know it, you're late and getting frustrated. Sound familiar? Well, Uber thinks it has a solution. The company just launched Uber Parking, a new feature that lets you reserve a parking spot directly through the Uber app before you even leave home. Yes, the same company that built its business around getting you into someone else's car now wants to help when you drive your own. And there's another interesting twist. Uber has plans for those parking garages that involve robotaxis.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

UBER LETS PARENTS WATCH TEEN RIDES LIVE

On Nov. 9, Uber announced the launch of Uber Parking, bringing parking reservations directly into its app. The feature follows Uber's acquisition of SpotHero, a popular parking reservation service. Through that deal, Uber gained access to a network of more than 13,000 parking garages, lots and valet locations across more than 400 cities in the United States and Canada.

So, instead of driving around looking for parking, you can search for an available spot near your destination. You can also see the price upfront, making it easier to decide whether driving makes financial sense. For someone heading into the city for dinner or trying to get to an important appointment, that could save some aggravation. And if you've ever paid a small fortune to park somewhere, you'll probably appreciate being able to compare prices before arriving.

Uber has made the process pretty simple. You can book parking using the same app you already use to request a ride.

Here's how it works:

Once you've booked, your digital parking pass appears inside the Uber app. Depending on the location, you'll either scan a QR code or enter through a system that recognizes your license plate. Uber also says you can extend reservations through the app if you need more time. Cancellation policies vary by parking facility. Some reservations qualify for a full refund if canceled before the scheduled start time. Always check the booking terms before paying.

One thing worth mentioning: Uber generally won't physically park your car for you. Unless you choose a valet location, you'll still be the one behind the wheel.

FAKE E-ZPASS EMAIL THREATENS $100 FINE OVER UNPAID TOLL

Uber Parking launched in 15 U.S. cities on Nov. 9.

Those cities are:

Uber plans to expand the service into additional markets. However, there's an important detail here. Although SpotHero operates across more than 400 cities, Uber Parking has not yet expanded throughout that entire network. Also, the new feature is still rolling out. So, even if you're in one of the launch cities, you may not see the Parking icon immediately. First, make sure you're using the latest version of the Uber app. You can also visit SpotHero's website to search for parking in areas where the Uber feature is unavailable.

Here's a little bonus if you already pay for Uber One. Uber says eligible members can earn 10% back in Uber One credits on qualifying parking reservations once their parking session is complete. You can use those credits toward future eligible Uber rides or Uber Eats orders. For example, if you spend $30 on a qualifying parking reservation, you could earn $3 in Uber One credits.

That may not sound like a fortune. However, if you're regularly parking downtown, those credits could add up. Just keep in mind that the 10% reward only applies to eligible reservations. You also need an active Uber One membership to qualify and redeem the credits. And remember, these are Uber credits rather than cash back to your bank account. Before booking, compare the total parking price with other nearby options. A cheaper garage could still save you more money than the rewards you'd earn.

Uber also sees parking garages as part of its future robotaxi business. Think about it. When a driverless taxi drops someone off, what happens next? If another passenger needs a ride nearby, that's easy enough. But what happens when nobody needs the car? Does it keep driving around until another request comes in? That could mean more empty vehicles on already crowded streets. Uber is reportedly exploring ways to use parking facilities as waiting areas for autonomous vehicles. Instead of driving around without passengers, robotaxis could pull into nearby garages and wait for their next assignment.

Then, when someone requests a ride, the vehicle could head out to pick them up. Uber believes that approach could reduce unnecessary driving and help lower operating costs. There's another potential benefit. Keeping autonomous vehicles in nearby facilities could make it easier to have them ready when demand increases. However, this remains a developing plan. Uber has not announced that every SpotHero garage will accommodate robotaxis, and the company has not provided a timeline for a broad rollout of these facilities. For now, the immediate focus remains helping people find parking for their own cars.

There's something else worth paying attention to here. For years, Uber built its business around giving people an alternative to driving. Now, the company wants you opening its app even when you plan to take your own car. Let's say you're going downtown for dinner. You could check the price of an Uber ride. Then, you could compare that with the cost of driving and parking.

If driving looks cheaper, you can reserve a space through Uber. If taking a ride makes more sense, you can book that instead. Either way, Uber stays part of your plans. And as autonomous vehicles become more common, the company could eventually use that same parking network to support its robotaxi partners. It's an interesting strategy, especially as Uber looks for more ways to keep people using its app.

The biggest benefit is pretty straightforward. You may be able to reserve parking before leaving home and spend less time driving around looking for an available spot. That could be especially useful when you're heading somewhere unfamiliar or trying to make a flight. However, there are a few things I'd recommend checking before you book.

Don't assume Uber offers the lowest rate. Check the final price against other parking options before paying. Also, make sure your reservation covers the time you'll actually need.

Some parking garages have height limits. If you drive a larger SUV or truck, check those restrictions before booking. Also, confirm the exact entrance address, which may differ from the garage's street address.

Some parking reservations can be canceled for free before they begin, but the rules vary by location. Review the specific garage's cancellation terms before booking. Once your reservation starts, Uber says it can no longer be canceled or refunded.

Some garages use QR codes for entry. That's convenient, but criminals have also placed fake QR codes on parking meters to trick drivers into visiting fraudulent payment websites. Use the parking pass provided directly through your Uber app rather than scanning an unfamiliar sticker. We've previously reported on how criminals use fake parking QR codes to steal money.

Even with a reservation, finding your car afterward can still be a headache. Fortunately, Google Maps and Apple Maps have tools that can help you remember where you parked. Our guide to finding your parked car with Maps explains how to set them up.

I think Uber is onto something here. Who hasn't wasted time driving around looking for parking, especially when you're already running late? Being able to reserve a spot before leaving home sounds pretty convenient. Of course, I'd want to make sure I'm getting a good price. But what really caught my attention is Uber's plan to use parking garages for robotaxis. Having driverless cars park between rides makes sense, especially if it means fewer empty vehicles clogging up our streets. Still, I wonder what happens when those garages start filling up with robotaxis. Will there be enough room for the rest of us? That's something I'll be watching as this technology takes off.

Would you trust Uber to handle your parking reservations, or do you worry that parking garages could eventually become crowded with robotaxis, leaving fewer spaces for the rest of us? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

articles.title: Putin launches Ukraine barrage hours after Trump meeting amid alleged Russian missile breach of NATO airspace
articles.summary:
Just hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin stood alongside President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a historic summit in China, Moscow unleashed one of its largest attacks on Ukraine, killing at least eight people, striking three major bridges in Kyiv and sending suspected Russian missiles and a drone into NATO-member Poland.

The massive overnight assault Friday came as the Trump administration announced progress toward expanding peace negotiations with Russia, exposing the stark contrast between the diplomatic optimism emerging from Thursday's meetings and the escalating war on the ground.

A European intelligence source told Fox News Digital that Putin is preparing an intensified winter military campaign and believes that a combination of sustained battlefield pressure and U.S.-led diplomatic negotiations could eventually force Ukraine to surrender additional territory.

TRUMP'S HISTORIC SUMMIT WITH XI, PUTIN MARKS DIPLOMATIC MILESTONE, BUT BREAKTHROUGHS REMAIN ELUSIVE

The source described the photograph of Putin standing alongside Trump and Xi as a long-sought diplomatic achievement for the Russian leader, even as Moscow prepares to increase pressure on Kyiv.

According to the source, Russia's calculation is that Ukraine could be compelled to accept territorial concessions by spring, particularly in the country's east.

"They are very convinced that by spring Ukrainians will give up," the source told Fox News Digital, describing what the source assessed to be Moscow's strategy.

The source also warned that Russian military pressure is increasing despite Ukraine's recent successful strikes against critical Russian infrastructure. "It's going to be a very difficult winter for Ukrainians," the source said.

Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove, former NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe, told Fox News Digital that the timing of Russia's latest assault should leave little doubt about Putin's intentions, arguing that the Russian leader has repeatedly responded to President Donald Trump's diplomatic overtures with renewed attacks on Ukraine.

"Putin never has been a partner for peace in Ukraine," he said. "And Putin will never be a partner for peace in the future for Ukraine." Breedlove said that Putin's objective is to subjugate Ukraine, install a leadership loyal to Moscow and exploit the country's resources.

RUSSIA PLOTTING 'MASSIVE STRIKE' DURING MIDTERMS, ZELENSKYY WARNS, URGES US TO STOP PUTIN

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, targeting the country's energy, transportation and logistical infrastructure.

The barrage killed six people in Kyiv and two in the western city of Lviv, while more than two dozen others were wounded, according to a Reuters' Nov. 20 report.

Three major bridges spanning the Dnipro River in Kyiv — the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, Darnytskyi and Pivdennyi bridges — were struck, disrupting transportation between the eastern and western sections of the capital.

Russian attacks also damaged railway infrastructure and energy facilities, triggering emergency power outages as temperatures drop ahead of winter.

In Lviv, two people were killed in a strike on the Sknyliv railway station, while additional injuries were reported following attacks on residential buildings and a hospital in other Ukrainian regions.

UKRAINE'S ZELENSKYY ON DEFYING US IN ATTACKING RUSSIAN OIL: 'OUR RESPONSE MUST BE PAINFUL'

Zelenskyy accused Moscow of using the attacks to compensate for what he described as military and diplomatic setbacks.

"This was one of the largest attacks," Zelenskyy said in a statement published on Telegram Friday.

Russia's Defense Ministry confirmed carrying out a massive operation, saying it targeted facilities connected to Ukraine's military-industrial complex, including missile and drone production sites and transportation infrastructure.

The competing claims about the targets and the extent of the damage could not be independently verified.

The strikes followed Putin's warning Thursday that Russia would retaliate against Ukraine for repeated attacks on the Kerch Bridge, which connects Russia with the occupied Crimean Peninsula.

Ukrainian forces launched three attacks on the strategic crossing in four days, damaging its road section and disrupting rail traffic.

The bridge, inaugurated by Putin in 2018, serves as both a transportation route and a powerful symbol of Moscow's control over Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014.

UKRAINE STRIKES 'ONE OF THE LARGEST OIL REFINERIES' IN SOUTHERN RUSSIA AHEAD OF PUTIN-TRUMP MEETING IN CHINA

The overnight assault also raised concerns beyond Ukraine's borders after Polish officials reported three separate incursions into the country's airspace.

Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said one of the objects was identified as a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, while another was believed to be a missile and the third likely a jet-powered drone.

Authorities were investigating debris near Nowy Lipowiec, Mołodycz and Rudnik nad Sanem in southeastern Poland.

"There has been a violation of Polish airspace and an incursion by objects from the Russian Federation," Kosiniak-Kamysz said, according to Reuters.

Poland said it would seek additional NATO assistance to secure the alliance's eastern flank.

Breedlove warned that the reported incursions into Polish airspace were part of a broader pattern of Russia testing NATO's resolve. "Mr. Putin will push further and further when there is no cost to him, when NATO doesn't respond, when the United States doesn't respond, in his mind, there is no reason to stop. He will continue," Breedlove told Fox News Digital.

UKRAINE RELEASES VIDEO SHOWING DAMAGE TO PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE FOLLOWING 'UNPRECEDENTED OPERATION' IN CRIMEA

The attacks came less than a day after the Trump administration announced what it described as progress toward a broader diplomatic framework involving Russia, Ukraine and European governments.

During talks in Berlin Thursday, U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said Moscow had agreed to engage in an expanded negotiating format that would include European representatives.

"Russia has agreed to engage in the multilateral format with the Europeans," Kushner said, according to Fox News Digital's Nov. 19 report.

Zelenskyy urged Washington to organize the next round of discussions quickly, insisting that European governments must play a full role in negotiations affecting the continent's security.

But Moscow's position remained less clear Friday, with Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov saying an invitation for European officials to visit Moscow did not mean they had been accepted into the existing U.S.-brokered negotiating format, according to The Associated Press.

The European intelligence source suggested Russia believes the diplomatic process itself could strengthen its negotiating position by allowing Moscow to broaden discussions beyond Ukrainian territory to the future security arrangements of Europe.

According to the source, Moscow is seeking to gain time, maintain military pressure and increasingly focus negotiations on wider European security questions.

The source also described Russian efforts to maintain troop numbers without announcing another large-scale nationwide mobilization.

"They have been able to avoid open mobilization, but they have hidden mobilization," the source said.

According to the source, Russian recruitment efforts include targeting people facing financial difficulties, debt or other social vulnerabilities, alongside continued recruitment from prisons.

RUSSIA'S PUTIN VOWS A RESPONSE 'FAR MORE PAINFUL' AFTER UKRAINE ATTACKS PRIZED BRIDGE IN CRIMEA

The source argued that Moscow is prioritizing manpower over the quality and training of new recruits.

"More quantity, less quality," the source said, warning that inadequately prepared recruits face a greater risk of being killed on the battlefield.

Those recruitment claims have not been independently verified by Fox News Digital.

The source's broader assessment was that Russia believes it can sustain military operations long enough to increase pressure on Ukraine's leadership to accept territorial concessions.

For Kyiv, the latest barrage demonstrated the immediate challenge facing U.S.-led peace efforts: negotiations are advancing while Moscow continues large-scale military operations and Ukraine strikes strategic targets deep inside Russian-held territory.

The events also highlighted the growing risks for NATO as the consequences of Russia's war extend beyond Ukraine's borders.

Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Senate foreign relations chairman warns of 'horrific trend' as Christians killed in Ethiopia
articles.summary:
The Republican chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee has warned of an ongoing ‘horrific trend’ of Christians being killed in Africa.

Earlier this month, at least 34 people, the majority said to be Ethiopian Orthodox Christians, were killed in a village in the Arsi Zone, about 250 miles southeast of Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa.

"The attacks on Christians in Ethiopia are a horrific trend," Sen. Jim Risch, R-Idaho, told Fox News Digital in a statement, adding, "The instability and violence in Ethiopia has grave consequences for Ethiopian civilians, the region and American interests."

NIGERIAN PASTOR HIGHLIGHTED BY TRUMP SAYS HE’S NEXT AFTER MILITIA KILLS HIS RELATIVES

Open Doors UK & Ireland told Fox News Digital there has been a string of killings in the area, with some 60 Orthodox Christians killed just two weeks before this attack in November. Open Doors is an international organization supporting persecuted Christians.

A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital they are aware of "reports of killing in Arsi Zone," adding: "Reports of civilian killings in Ethiopia demand action. We call for independent investigations and accountability."

The Addis Standard online news outlet reported gunmen approached St. Mary’s Church in Endeto, Robe District, and at the main entrance shouted "Surrender" before opening fire. Worshipers here are from the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. Local security guards, who are said to have fired back to protect community members, are believed to be among the dead.

One resident told the Addis Standard, "If you asked me right now, I have no hope of staying here because I would choose to flee for long-term survival."

The identity of the attackers has not yet been confirmed. An attack last month has been attributed locally to the Oromo Liberation Army, designated in Ethiopia as a terrorist organization.

The State Department, quoting the Ethiopian government’s 2007 census, the most recent available, stated the country’s population is 63% Christian. One local source reports though that three of those who died in this latest attack were Muslim.

SUPER BOWL CHAMP BEN WATSON SPEAKS OUT ON CHRISTIAN NIGERIAN PERSECUTION, DOUBLE-STANDARDS AND TRUMP'S IMPACT

Ethiopia is ranked 36 on Open Doors’ World Watch List of countries where Christians are most persecuted. The organization stated "Open Doors condemns the violence against Orthodox Christians and calls on the Government of Ethiopia to take proactive measures to protect vulnerable civilians from attacks by armed groups operating in the area. Reports from the field point to horrific brutality against Orthodox Christians in parts of the Arsi zone of Oromia."

The statement continued, "We urge the federal government to protect vulnerable communities, including Orthodox Christians, particularly in areas where armed groups are active. We also call on the government to hold perpetrators accountable and help all those affected rebuild their lives."

ANOTHER CHRISTIAN COMMUNITY AT RISK IN AFRICA AS EXTREMISTS AND WAR TAKE THEIR TOLL

Open Doors states the recent attacks in the area started in 2025, when 25 people were killed. 

The attacks have ramped up this year:

In February, attackers stormed a church and a market in East Arsi, killing more than 20 Orthodox Christians and one Muslim guard.

In March, 21 people were reportedly killed in East Arsi Zone.

In May, the 101-year-old Teleta Holy Gabriel Church was destroyed and 50 killed in multiple attacks.

In October, 14 people were killed in Gora Singo and in the Arsi Zone, 46 were killed in multiple attacks. This led to the U.S. Ambassador to Ethiopia Ervin J. Masinga posting, "Such horrific attacks against any group must stop."

In November, at least 34 were killed in Endeto.

Senate Foreign Affairs Chairman Risch added, "It is imperative that Ethiopia find a way to manage its domestic affairs in a way that addresses longstanding grievances and promotes sustained peace."

With fighting continuing in several parts of the country, especially in the border area around Eritrea, the State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "Fighting in several regions of Ethiopia is a concern. We urge all parties to protect civilians and resolve disputes through dialogue."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Ethiopian government, but received no response.

articles.title: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO

Nvidia's stock surged 32%, adding nearly $1 trillion to its market cap while the rest of Wall Street also rallied.

articles.title: Libya's east seeks UN probe into claims Ukrainian military present in west
articles.summary: Authorities in divided Libya's east called on Monday for the United Nations to investigate claims that Ukrainian forces were present in the country's west, as they lodged a complaint over Ukrainian attacks on two Russian ships off Benghazi. The strikes on Sunday, claimed by Kyiv, come as Ukraine steps up strikes against Russia far from the front lines of their war. FRANCE 24's Emerald Maxwell reports.

articles.title: Trump backs Nvidia boss's return but top Democrat vows probe
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump praised Nvidia's decision Monday to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive, as top Senate Democrat Chuck Schumer vowed to investigate potential wrongdoing amid mounting national security concerns. Trump also posted a doctored version of the famous photograph of him raising his fist after surviving a 2024 assassination attempt, replacing himself with Huang, who brandished a red bra beneath an Nvidia flag. FRANCE 24's Fraser Jackson reports from Washington.

articles.title: How far will Ukraine war spread? Kyiv targets Russian vessels in Libya
articles.summary: Talk about spillover. In the Libyan port of Benghazi, Ukraine claiming responsibility for the sinkings first of a Russian warship and then a cargo vessel. That’s on top of the sanctioned ship struck in the Baltic Sea that’s since strayed into Finland’s waters. Legitimate targets?

articles.title: Ukraine claims it sank Russian warship off Libya
articles.summary: Ukraine on Monday claimed it was behind strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya, including one that sank a modern warship, in the latest spillover from Moscow's invasion. The attacks on Sunday near the Libyan port of Benghazi come at a time when Ukraine has stepped up its daring strikes against Russia far from the frontlines in retaliation for Moscow's deadly invasion. FRANCE 24's Gulliver Cragg reports from Kyiv.

articles.title: Nvidia reinstates Huang as CEO after Trump intervention
articles.summary: Nvidia on Monday reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive in a stunning reversal that President Donald Trump said followed his own direct contacts with the company's board. Huang resigned two weeks ago over an affair with a woman whom US intelligence agencies suspect of spying for China, a departure that sent Wall Street tumbling and stoked fears for a US economy reliant on the AI investment boom. FRANCE 24's Carys Garland and Wassim Cornet report.

articles.title: 'Maintain control': UN chief calls for creation of global AI safety framework within a year
articles.summary: UN chief Antonio Guterres on Monday urged countries to agree on the creation of a global framework for managing the dangers posed by artificial intelligence within one year. Speaking at a summit in Barbados, he warned that taming the technology is vital if humanity is to stay in charge of its own future.

articles.title: 'Deeply shocked': Gisèle Pelicot to sue publisher after nude photos used in book campaign
articles.summary: French feminist icon Gisèle Pelicot, who became a worldwide symbol against sexual violence during the 2024 rape trials against her husband and dozens of other men, said Monday she will take legal action after nude images of her were sent out without her permission to publicise a psychoanalyst's book on coercive control.

articles.title: Finland summons Russian ambassador after suspected airspace violation

Helsinki also condemned Moscow's escalating strikes on civilian targets in Ukraine.

articles.summary: Belgium's prime minister on Monday set a new year-end deadline for his coalition government to agree a cost-cutting budget or face collapse. The announcement came as a national strike against the planned cuts grounded all flights in and out of Belgium. Public transport, schools and other public services also faced disruption. France 24's Dave Keating has the latest from Brussels.

articles.title: Iran's courts order US to pay $290 billion in damages

articles.title: Behind COP31 failure: A showdown over fossil fuel interests
articles.summary: Several countries and environmental groups expressed fury at the collapse of the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey on Sunday, amid a dramatic failure to thrash out an agreement, two days after the summit was scheduled to end. Oil-producing states blocked any mention of phasing out fossil fuels – the root cause of the climate crisis – with the EU then refusing to back a weakened text. Our Environment Editor Valerie Dekimpe tells us more.

articles.title: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO

articles.summary: French presidential candidate David Lisnard has surprised many by surpassing former prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal in a recent voter intention pole. The mayor of Cannes is running on an ultra-liberal platform and has gained a large following on social media, but some critics say he lacks the national experience needed for the Elysée.

articles.title: France's socioeconomic crisis: Macron 'trying to impose fiscal discipline on his successor'
articles.summary: Charli James is pleased to welcome Andrew Smith, Historian of Modern France and Lecturer in Liberal Arts at Queen Mary University of London. He argues that Emmanuel Macron is seeking to "impose fiscal discipline on his successor as president" after "presiding over quite a substantial deterioration in the public finances." For Smith, the difficulty is that "it's easier to agree on the need for fiscal discipline than on who should pay for it or should have the authority to actually determine it." He suggests that the far right "may play the deciding role" in whether the proposal succeeds, potentially presenting itself as "solving the problems created by Macron's two terms."

articles.title: Dhaka bursting at the seams: Bangladeshi capital faces public health, housing crisis
articles.summary: The Bangladeshi capital Dhaka is one of the most densely populated places on Earth, with over 35,000 people per square kilometre, compared with 20,000 in Paris. articles.title: Finland summons Russian ambassador over suspected helicopter incursion
articles.summary:
The Finnish Ministry of Foreign Affairs summoned Moscow’s ambassador to Helsinki Monday afternoon over its suspicions a Russian helicopter violated Finnish airspace Saturday.

The Russian helicopter was sighted at the southern coastal town of Loviisa shortly after midday. The Ministry of Defense said the aircraft encroached on Finland’s territory by some 4.1 kilometers.

“Russia’s dangerous and reckless actions in Europe are unacceptable,” the foreign ministry said in a statement on X. “We strongly condemn Russia’s illegal war of aggression and its escalating strikes against civilian targets in Ukraine. We stand in solidarity with Denmark, Poland and our other European partners.”

Several other European countries have criticized Russia over air incursions with helicopters and drones in recent months. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned on Sept. 17 that Russia could launch drone or missile strikes against countries that support Ukraine, and try to pass them off as accidents.

Finnish Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen said the suspected incursion may have been related to “rescue or monitoring operations” involving the Russian cargo ship Sparta II, which was damaged by a Ukrainian drone attack in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday morning.

The Finnish Border Guard said it had towed the ship from Finnish waters to Russia Sunday afternoon.

“Ukraine has the right to defend itself against Russia’s illegal aggression,” the foreign ministry added in the statement alongside Monday’s statement.

Moscow has not yet publicly responded to Finland’s summoning of its ambassador.

articles.title: Britain’s runaway Brexit debate is back
articles.summary:
LONDON — Andy Burnham assured Britain on Monday that he has no plans to “bang on about Europe” — but that conversation is now in full flow whether he likes it or not.

Questions about the U.K.’s long-term future relationship with the EU dominated a statement to parliament by Burnham in which — officially, at least — he updated MPs on three technical deals on food standards, youth mobility and emissions trading that he announced at Friday’s U.K.-EU summit.

Those questions also loomed over a business conference 300 metres away, attended by Burnham and England’s four other main party leaders and hosted by the Confederation of British Industry.

On the CBI stage Ed Davey, leader of the pro-EU Liberal Democrats, boasted he could renegotiate entry to single market and customs union “within a year.” Two hours later Nigel Farage, leader of the anti-EU Reform UK, told business delegates that Brexit “may well be” the issue that reverses his party’s falling poll rating. In the media, five former prime ministers have warned against reopening old wounds.

And in the Commons chamber, Burnham was grilled by a parade of veterans from both sides of the Brexit wars that dominated Britain for years after its 2016 EU referendum. 

The prime minister told one veteran Conservative Euroskeptic it would be “unthinkable” to rejoin the bloc without a new referendum — the first time he had confirmed that view — and denied Britain would rejoin the European single currency.

Not for nothing did Kemi Badenoch tell the CBI that Burnham was “opening Pandora’s box.” The leader of the opposition Conservative Party, which lost two prime ministers over the European debate, told business leaders: “The last thing this country needs is another five years of division, distraction and arguments about Brexit.”

Talking about Brexit, again

It is but a taste of the fractious debate unfolding for Burnham, who two months ago started a deliberately open-ended conversation about Britain’s future relationship with Europe.

The prime minister has already slowed down that process, promising to present “options” for the future relationship in mid-December instead of roughly this week.

That will give way to an “informal brainstorm” with the EU ahead of a summit in late 2027, with Burnham only promising to forge further ahead — if indeed he does — in Labour’s next general election manifesto, due by mid-2029.

“There will be no banging on about Europe from this side, or a running commentary. Instead, just a calm, constructive, and pragmatic consideration of what is in Britain’s interests in the long term,” Burnham told MPs.

The prime minister appeared to suggest that his personal enthusiasm for rejoining the EU in his lifetime could wane if, for example, the far-right politician Marine Le Pen wins the French presidency. “Europe could change again in the next year, 18 months, and we’ll have to obviously watch how life changes,” he said.

At a CBI breakfast Burnham attended with 40 executives, a large chunk of the conversation was about his upcoming (mostly domestic) 10-year plan for Britain, according to one person in the room, granted anonymity like others in this piece to speak freely. But existential questions about Britain’s future in Europe were everywhere — and everyone had their own answers.

To Burnham’s many supporters in his Labour Party, he has taken ownership of a debate that dominates British politics anyway, and in doing so has improved Labour’s standing in seats where Labour is battling the pro-EU Lib Dems and Green Party.

One Labour MP said: “It was not going to be possible for us to avoid talking about our future relationship with Europe, and Andy has got out ahead of some of it.”

Peter Kyle, who was business secretary under Burnham’s predecessory Keir Starmer, added in the Commons: “You can’t reopen something that never closed in the first place.”

Others in his party are more skeptical. One pro-EU Labour MP in a pro-EU seat said it felt like “madness” to restart such a fractious conversation. 

‘Damaging indecision’

The new Brexit debate has been fueled by Burnham’s tendency to speak his mind without anticipating every consequence.

Conservative Shadow Foreign Secretary Tom Tugendhat told the LBC news outlet on Monday morning that Burnham had privately made “extremely clear” to French President Emmanuel Macron — during a visit in September — that “his entire plan was to re-join the European Union.” (A government official told POLITICO they had seen no evidence to substantiate such a claim.)

The kerfuffle prompted one minister, to joke, deadpan, before Burnham’s statement in Parliament: “Wait for the statement. Maybe he’ll announce we are going back in [to the EU]. Who knows?”

Burnham and his allies in the Cabinet — several of whom have personal reservations about rejoining the EU — have recently sought to regain control of the narrative.

Louise Haigh, his de facto deputy, told Monday’s CBI conference that the Friday deals were “the extent to which we can go” before the next general election and Labour would “come back to” options for the future relationship at its manifesto.

Burnham’s official spokesperson added: “I’m not going to set a deadline for those discussions. The prime minister has said they will take time, and it’s right we engage seriously before setting out an assessment.”

That slowing-down in itself might create a new headache for Burnham, however — business uncertainty.

One chief executive said they believed Burnham’s actions were pointing toward an early election. “We can’t afford to have another 2 or 3 year conversation,” the exec said. “I was an ultra-remainer but even I am not sure if I want to restart a whole national debate.”

Another senior figure in one of Britain’s largest firms said “for the first time in my life I agree with Theresa May” — the ex-prime minister who urged Burnham not to reopen old wounds on Sunday.

Martin McTague, the Labour peer and former chair of the Federation of Small Businesses, argued the government was being “pragmatic” but he believed rejoining is a “remote possibility and it would depend a lot on the conditions.” He said the business community is divided, with food and drink firms “liberated” but others nervous about aligning too firmly with EU standards on artificial intelligence.

McTague added: “We suffered three years of indecision and political arguments about the future of Europe, and that was extremely damaging. So I hope we’re not facing three years of indecision about this … In a way, it’s like an echo of the referendum. We left without knowing what we were going to be faced with. Now we’ve been asked to rejoin without knowing what the terms are.”

The FSB’s members are split on Brexit. Executive Director Craig Beaumont said: “We do not support reheating 2016 and a divisive referendum that would sap political energy away from sorting out the issues small businesses face. [The food standards deal] builds on what’s there.”

CBI Director-General Rain Newton-Smith used her speech Monday to urge Burnham to have the “courage” to pursue a specific model of European alignment in the long-term.

Speaking to POLITICO afterward, though, Newton-Smith conceded it would be “quite a long process.” She added: “I think the thing that will matter most is that we had the U.K.-EU summit, we had a deal on Friday. How that deal is delivered is the thing that’s on the table and probably matters most.”

Dave Bench, the chief executive of pesticides industry group Croplife UK, added: “How close the government wants to get to the EU is not the critical issue for our companies. We need certainty now on the law and requirements, and how those will be implemented.”

‘Banging on about Europe’

Even doing that will be no walk in the park.

Burnham’s government is due to introduce legislation implementing the summit outcome this Thursday. EU officials have threatened to sink the deals if both sides cannot agree a cut to EU students’ tuition fees in the U.K. (Burnham declined to confirm if he would compensate universities for the reduction in fees.)

The U.K. must also decide whether to align with EU tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles to benefit from Brussels’ Made in Europe scheme. Haigh dropped a further hint Monday that Britain could do so, telling the CBI “we share that concern” about China flooding the market.

Aligning strongly with the EU would bring into question Britain’s pitch to be a global broker on AI safety. Haigh told the BBC Monday: “We have diverged on AI and financial services, and that has driven growth in our economy. So we need to consider these things when we consider our next steps in the relationship with the EU.”

Conservative opponents also suggest full membership would throw Burnham’s pitch for greater “public control” over key utilities into doubt. Former Environment Secretary Thérèse Coffey said Monday that the European Court of Justice had repeatedly ruled against governments holding “golden shares” in major industries.

It may be little wonder that Haigh, who is 39, swerved saying whether she would support rejoining the EU in her lifetime. “The problem with this lifetime framing is it sort of makes us all wonder when we’re going to die,” she told the CBI.

The issue for Haigh and others is that the Brexit debate has outlived many deaths and will outlive many more — especially now that Burnham has put it back on the table.

It is now 20 years since the former Conservative Prime Minister David Cameron urged his party to stop “banging on about Europe.” Just like his Cameron, Burnham may find the conversation is not always his to control.

articles.title: Spain turns against Sánchez, POLITICO poll finds
articles.summary:
Spain’s election will be dominated by the cost of living, housing and strong views about whether Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez should stay or go, according to new POLITICO polling originally published in Madrid Playbook.

On Sunday, Spaniards will head to the polls to vote in an election that could hand a win to the center-right People’s Party, ousting Sánchez and the European Union’s last major Socialist-led government after eight years in power.

Recent polls project it will be a tight race, with the PP neck-and-neck with Sánchez’s Socialists at around 30% and far-right Vox in third place at around 18%.

The prime minister had already come under pressure over his government’s handling of the Ceuta migration crisis over the summer and corruption cases involving his family, but he finally called a snap election in early October following nationwide protests about unaffordable housing.

A survey pollster PF Global carried out for POLITICO last week shows housing remains a vulnerable area for Sánchez. In the poll, it topped the list of the prime minister’s failures, slightly ahead of migration and the Ceuta crisis.

While PP and Vox voters were more likely to say migration had been Sánchez’s biggest failure, the prime minister’s own support base was more likely to list housing.

Some 40% of people who said they’d vote for the Socialist Party and over half of those backing the leftist alliance Broad Front said he’d fallen short on housing.

Across the board, about one-third of Spaniards in the poll said cost of living would drive their vote. But different parties’ voters had different priorities: For PP and Vox voters, migration was a key factor in their choice, whereas Socialist Party voters said housing and healthcare would steer their vote more.

At the same time, all parties are struggling to convince voters they are well placed to tackle key campaign issues.

One-third of respondents said they trust Vox the most to tackle migration. On other topics, parties were largely preferred by their own voters. Asked which party they trusted most to tackle corruption, the most common answer across the board was “None.”

The numbers suggest personal opinions of Sánchez will play a central role in voting decisions Sunday.

One-third of respondents said parties’ positions on key issues would determine how they vote, but nearly one-third said removing Sánchez from power would be a key motivation when voting.

Nearly 60% of people who plan to vote for the PP and Vox said this was a reason for their choice.

Over 80% of PP and Vox voters also supported a governing coalition between the two parties to topple the prime minister.

Conversely, nearly one-third said they’d vote tactically to keep a particular party out of government. Among Socialist and Broad Front voters, that share rose to 44%.

The POLITICO poll showed that Sunday’s election won’t be so much a popularity contest as a reflection of who voters dislike less.

None of the three major party leaders received large support in the survey. About 30% each reported positive views about PP’s Alberto Núñez Feijóo, Vox leader Santiago Abascal and Sánchez.

Over half said they held a negative view of Sánchez, while 42% said they thought negatively of Feijóo.

The POLITICO Poll was conducted by PF Global from Nov. 15 to 17, surveying 2,454 Spanish adults online. Results were weighted by age and gender, region, educational attainment and past vote. The overall margin of sampling error is ±2.0 percentage points. Smaller subgroups have higher margins of error.

articles.title: Rejoining EU without referendum is ‘unthinkable,’ says Andy Burnham
articles.summary:
LONDON — Rejoining the European Union without first holding a public referendum would be “unthinkable” for the U.K., Andy Burnham told MPs Monday.

The British prime minister has said Brexit “has not worked” and that rejoining could be on the table in the next parliament.

But asked during a parliamentary debate on Monday afternoon whether it would be “unthinkable” to rejoin without a fresh referendum, he replied: “Yes, it would be unthinkable.”

It is the first time the prime minister has ruled out the prospect of returning Britain to the bloc without holding a special vote on the matter.

Burnham was speaking days after negotiating three new international agreements to ramp up ties with the bloc at a summit in Brussels.

Addressing MPs during Monday’s debate, the prime minister accused his critics of being “stuck in the past” by refusing to reopen the issue.

Burnham argued that Britain’s Conservative Party needed to “face up” to mistakes it made on Brexit after several former Tory prime ministers warned him away from reversing the decision.

“They’ve brought out a line-up of former prime ministers, one after another, to say that we shouldn’t even begin to talk about Brexit,” he told the House of Commons.

“Those who say we shouldn’t talk about Brexit risk leaving Britain stuck in the past with a substandard set of arrangements. Instead, we are putting Britain back on a better path and bringing back the hope that has been missing for too long.”

In response to questioning from opposition leader Kemi Badenoch, Burnham said the public would see “a Conservative Party today that cannot face up to those mistakes they made years ago, mistakes that damaged Britain and left us where we are today.”

The Tory leader hit back, accusing the prime minister of having “changed his tune” on the issue after being elected at a by-election earlier this year in the town of Makerfield on “a promise that he would not reopen the debate on Brexit.”

Homing in on Labour Cabinet splits over the issue, she said Burnham was pursuing a policy “his own chancellor and health secretary have publicly denounced.”

“Forget uniting the country. He can’t even unite his own Cabinet,” she declared.

Nigel Farage, one of the leading campaigners for Brexit in the 2016 referendum, told POLITICO’s Anne McElvoy that Burnham’s push for closer ties with the EU “may well be” the cause that reignites his right-wing political party Reform UK — which lost its poll lead over the ruling Labour Party during the summer. 

“Frankly, if Andy Burnham wants a full-on fight on this issue then someone please hold my jacket. I’m looking forward to it,” he said in an interview at a Confederation of British Industry conference Monday.

The U.K. held a referendum on its membership of the EU on June 23, 2016 in which it voted to leave by 52 percent to 48 percent. The decision caused the immediate resignation of then-Prime Minister David Cameron and fired the starting gun on more than four years of negotiations over the terms of departure.

This story has been updated to include comments from Nigel Farage.

articles.title: Lib Dem leader claims he could negotiate EU single market access ‘within a year’
articles.summary:
LONDON — A Liberal Democrat government could renegotiate Britain’s reentry into the single market and customs union “within a year,” the party’s leader Ed Davey claimed Monday.

“I think the negotiations would be incredibly easy,” Davey told POLITICO in a fireside chat at the Confederation of British Industry annual conference. “I think you could probably have it done in record speed … within a year,” he said.

The centrist party — which is the third largest in the House of Commons — has long advocated for Britain to aim to rejoin the single market and customs union. The ruling Labour Party pledged not to join either in its 2024 winning election manifesto.

Davey said Britain has been through the process before and rejoining existing frameworks would be easier than negotiating a bespoke deal.

The economic benefits would start flowing even before Britain was back inside the single market and customs union, he added.

Davey’s comments came days after Andy Burnham’s Labour government secured deals on agrifood, energy and a youth mobility at a landmark U.K.-EU summit in Brussels on Friday.

The Lib Dem leader said his party had been calling for such a deal “five years ago,” but he argued that the world has since moved on.

“We need a lot more growth, and a lot of growth comes from trade, and I think actually this is quite a timid deal,” he said, adding that it remains within the confines of Boris Johnson’s Trade and Cooperation Agreement.

Burnham has pledged to set out possible options for even closer ties to the EU next month, with rejoining the customs union or single market — or even holding another referendum to rejoin the bloc — among the options floated.  

Asked about the possibility of a second referendum, Davey said it would not be so easy.

 “We need to explain to British people the huge benefits of Europe before we get to that point,” he said. “I think the Europeans will need a bit of persuading, given the awful history of the last few years.”

articles.title: EU targets Russian ex-soldiers, banks and sports in new sanctions push
articles.summary:
BRUSSELS — The EU wants to target former Russian soldiers, banks, crypto platforms and sports teams in its 22nd sanctions package against Moscow since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced on Monday.

“We’re giving Ukraine the strength to secure a peace. And Russia, every reason to choose it,” von der Leyen said in a prerecorded video message launching the package.

The Commission’s proposals will now be negotiated by EU countries, with several diplomats telling POLITICO that they aim to reach an agreement by the end of the year.

One major measure would restrict visas for former Russian soldiers. The EU agreed on a legal framework for the restrictions in its previous sanctions package over the summer but has yet to put them into effect.

“Russian ex-combatants pose a security risk to Europe. They cannot be allowed to wander freely across our countries,” von der Leyen said, citing a recent escalation in covert Russian operations in Europe.

The Commission also wants to add 70 vessels to its sanctions list targeting Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, which Moscow uses to export oil and other commodities.

European companies would also be barred from repairing Russian refineries damaged by Ukrainian drone attacks. EU citizens would no longer be allowed to sit on the boards of Russian companies.

On sports, the Commission is proposing to bar Russian teams and athletes from competing in the bloc, a move that would prevent Russia from returning to next year’s ice hockey world championship in Germany.

“We propose to ban the display of official Russian symbols. We will also restrict financial flows from Russian sponsors to European based sports and cultural associations,” von der Leyen said.

An arbitration court had ruled that the International Ice Hockey Federation lacked sufficient grounds to exclude Russia from the tournament.

Closing sanctions loopholes and cracking down on shadow finance is another focus of the package. The Commission wants to disconnect 60 more banks from international payment systems and target cryptocurrency and payment networks used to circumvent sanctions.

“We will focus on Russia, but also include third countries that help Russia to evade our sanctions,” von der Leyen said.

The EU has previously been cautious about directly targeting third countries, but von der Leyen said the new measures would help “align with international partners.”

The latest proposals follow a difficult year for EU sanctions policy. A previous package was held up for weeks over restrictions on liquefied natural gas shipments, while France delayed the renewal of an existing sanctions framework over a national security dispute, demanding the removal of two Russian billionaires from the sanctions list.

Last week, the Commission announced the creation of a dedicated sanctions office to oversee the design, drafting and coordination of restrictive measures.

articles.title: Ukraine takes the war against Russia far from its borders
articles.summary:
KYIV — Ukraine regularly hits targets deep inside Russia; now it’s admitting to an attack far beyond the war zone, in North Africa.

The attack — an effort to harm Russia’s ability to project power into distant regions — highlights Ukraine’s growing technological prowess but it also carries the risk of diplomatic blowback against Kyiv.

The Security Service of Ukraine, or SBU, said its forces on Sunday sank the Russian corvette Merkury anchored in the Libyan port of Benghazi. The Angara, a Russian dry cargo vessel that Kyiv claimed was being used to transport weapons, was also struck.

In another attack, a cargo ship sailing under the Russian flag was damaged by a drone attack in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday morning, the defense ministry in Helsinki said. Finnish authorities said that Ukraine carried out the attack in international waters; however, Kyiv has not admitted responsibility.

Broadly, Ukraine has expanded its attacks against Russian targets well outside the war zone in an effort to exert more pain on Moscow, said Mykola Bielieskov, research fellow at the Ukrainian National Institute for Strategic Studies.

“Given the fact that frontline operations and strikes against oil refineries and the defense-industrial complex are insufficient to compel the enemy to end the war immediately and unconditionally, Ukraine is seeking additional tools of pressure,” he said.

The Libya operation is the first time Ukraine has claimed credit for such a distant strike, but there was little point in denying it after the Benghazi government posted videos of the attacks.

There are also accusations that Ukrainian forces have long been active in other theaters.

Earlier this year, Greece said it would launch an investigation after a naval drone carrying explosives was discovered in the Ionian Sea. Greek and Ukrainian media identified it as likely a Ukrainian-made Magura drone.

Sudan, Mali and Niger have accused Ukrainian special operatives of getting involved in their internal affairs; Russia’s mercenary troops are present in all three countries. Kyiv has strongly denied those accusations.

“These operations have demonstrated the remarkable agility and boldness of Kyiv’s intelligence services in attacking vulnerable parts of the Kremlin’s sprawling security apparatus and its global footprint,” said the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in a report issued last year, adding: “The persistence of such attacks suggests that Kyiv will continue to look for ways to punish Russia beyond the front line.”

Libyan anger

After Sunday’s attacks, local Libyan authorities filed a complaint to the United Nations and demanded an investigation.

“We call on Ukraine to provide an official explanation of its military activities in Libya,” said Osama Hammad, the head of Libya’s parliament-appointed government.

Ukraine said the operation was carried out from the sea. A so-called mothership transported seven Ukrainian-made sea drones to the area and launched them, the SBU said.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov on Monday denounced the Gulf of Finland attack.

“All coastal countries are undoubtedly concerned about this. It is very dangerous. It is escalating tensions in the region,” he said, adding: “Of course, we hope that the Baltic states will use their influence to dissuade the Kyiv regime from continuing these dangerous terrorist practices.”

Even Kyiv’s closest allies are squeamish about attacks on commercial shipping.

“Ukraine, of course, has the right to strike military targets, targets used for military purposes in Russia, in order to weaken Russian attacks on Ukraine,” German Defense Minster Boris Pistorius said Monday. “At the same time, Ukraine naturally also bears a particular responsibility. The war must not spread to the Baltic Sea.”

On the Libya attacks, Peskov said the Kremlin has “noticed [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy’s statement on ship destruction,” but refused to issue any further comments.

While there is no debate that the Merkury is a military vessel, Kyiv said that the cargo vessel was also a legitimate target.

“The Defense Forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea,” the SBU said. “Such unique special operations disrupt the enemy’s logistical capabilities and force Russia to pay for its aggression, even at a strategic distance from Ukraine.”

Ukraine has not claimed credit for the March sinking of the Russian-flagged Arctic Metagaz LNG tanker sailing between Libya and Malta, said Igor Semyvolos, executive director of the Association of Middle East Studies think tank. Moscow says Kyiv was to blame.

“A tanker is a civilian vessel; striking one would raise environmental concerns and lead to complaints with the International Maritime Organization. A corvette, by contrast, is an aggressor’s warship — a legitimate military target. It is safe to claim responsibility for such a strike,” Semyvolos said.

The sinking of the Metagaz did send a cautionary signal to Moscow, said Sebastian Rötters, sanctions campaigner at Urgewald, an NGO, forcing Russia to ship its LNG “onto longer and more expensive routes.”

“The latest strikes near Benghazi show that risks have not disappeared,” he said.

Zelenskyy underscored Monday that the Libyan attacks were part of a broader campaign aimed at getting Moscow to end the war.

“Russia can feel our response all the way from western Siberia, where its oil refineries are burning, to the coast of Libya, where its warships are sinking,” he said. “And we have offered Russia steps to reduce the fighting dozens, dozens of times. And we have never been the ones to raise the stakes.”

Martina Sapio contributed to this report.

This article has been updated.

articles.title: Badenoch: Rejoining EU won’t fix Britain’s economic woes
articles.summary:
LONDON — Britain’s economy needs a reboot and reopening the debate on its relationship with the European Union won’t solve it, Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch told business chiefs Monday.

Speaking just a few days after Andy Burnham’s government reached a series of deals with the EU in a landmark summit, Badenoch accused the British prime minister of choosing to “look backwards” on a topic which creates uncertainty and prevents politicians from focusing on economic growth.

“I know I speak for the majority of people when I say reopening the Brexit debate is the last thing our country needs right now. There are many more urgent priorities,” Badenoch told the Confederation of British Industry’s annual conference in London Monday.

“The last thing this country needs is another five years of division, distraction and arguments about Brexit,” she added.

The Tory leader echoed several former prime ministers, including Tony Blair and Theresa May, who in recent days cautioned Burnham over reopening Brexit. Badenoch said Burnham is opening a “Pandora’s box” and noted that “five prime ministers, not just Conservative ones … have told him that the rejoining the EU conversation he’s opening is not the right one.”

Friday’s discussions with the EU focused on deals on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth visas scheme. Burnham has said he wants Britain to rejoin the EU in his lifetime but has not committed his government to pursuing membership.

Badenoch said the U.K. should work with the EU on issues including defense, security and trade, but argued renewed membership of the EU “is not going to solve our recurring problems,” including lower projected growth and the government spending more than £100 billion servicing its debt.

“Something bad is happening in our economy, and rejoining the EU is not going to fix it. Nor will staying outside the EU automatically fix it either. Britain needs to be more ambitious than just changing our relationship with Brussels,” she said.

Instead, Badenoch said the U.K. should continue looking to the rest of the world rather than “locking yourself into one market,” adding that “Europe will always remain an important market, but it is not the market of the future.”

Manifesto

The Conservative leader’s speech came after First Secretary of State Louise Haigh dodged questions about her personal view on Britain rejoining the EU.

“We’ll come back to what that might look like at the manifesto,” she told the same conference Monday.

But she earlier cautioned Britain needs to consider the growth created from diverging with the EU on AI and financial services regulations.

“I really note Tony Blair’s caution around AI, because we have diverged on AI and financial services, and that has driven growth in our economy,” she said of warnings from the ex-prime minister that Brussels must reform and allow more innovation on technology if Britain is to rejoin.

“So we need to consider these things when we consider our next steps in the relationship with the EU,” Haigh said.

Speaking to broadcasters on Monday morning, Burnham dismissed the warnings from former prime ministers May, as well as David Cameron and Rishi Sunak, on reopening Brexit talks.

“I’m not a prime minister that’s going to be stuck in the past,” Burnham said. “I want to lead Britain forward to a more hopeful future, get the economy growing again, get cost of living down for people, lower energy bills.”

articles.title: Macron moves to ‘trap’ successors with new budget rule
articles.summary:
PARIS — French President Emmanuel Macron is pushing to enshrine strict rules on deficit spending in his country’s constitution before leaving office in May.

An adviser to Macron, who was granted anonymity to discuss the plan like others quoted in this report, confirmed that the Elysée is looking at adopting a so-called golden rule in the constitution to “demonstrate the country’s ability to maintain sound public finances over the long term.”

France is saddled with nearly €3.6 trillion in debt amounting to 119% of gross domestic product and a stubbornly high budget deficit projected to come in at 5.4% of GDP this year.

But Macron’s opponents — and even some of his allies — aren’t buying that logic.

“The fact that Emmanuel Macron waited until his tenth budget with a massive deficit under his presidency to consider this tells a lot about a president who waited until he had emptied the coffers before deciding to lock them up,” conservative candidate Bruno Retailleau wrote on X.

“It’s as if he were saying, I pursued a policy that led to deficits, but now I want to pressure my successor to follow a rule that I didn’t accept,” said an adviser to a lawmaker from Macron’s party.

An unofficial adviser who speaks regularly with Macron said the French leader is “trying to trap” presidential candidates who have floated their own constitutional spending limits — like far-right leader Marine Le Pen and center-right former PM Edouard Philippe — by forcing them to pick a side in a potential vote.

The first Macron adviser quoted above said the model for their proposal would be a measure adopted in 2011 but never formally enacted that would have required governments to lay out their deficit trajectory for three years — not the “golden rule” of government spending as it’s normally understood.

The rule is typically defined as a fiscal policy in which governments only borrow to invest, but in French public discourse the phrase is often used to refer to constitutionally mandated deficit targets like those in place in Germany and Italy.

In France, constitutional reforms can only be adopted by referendum or in a vote that receives a three-fifths majority of the country’s two chambers of parliament. A former aide to an MP who still advises on parliamentary procedure said such a measure could pass, possibly by as many as 20 votes if all centrists and conservatives backed it and Le Pen’s far-right National Rally abstained.

Le Pen, the front-runner in the race to succeed Macron next spring, said Sunday that she was waiting to see details on Macron’s plan before deciding whether to back it. Retailleau backed the idea while questioning its timing.

Philippe, who was once seen as the best-placed moderate to beat Le Pen but is struggling in the polls, said last year he supported holding a referendum on constitutional budget restrictions.

Far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who polls show is on track to face Le Pen in the presidential election runoff, is likely to oppose the measure. Lawmaker Eric Coquerel, a prominent member of Mélenchon’s party who chairs the National Assembly’s finance committee, said the proposal would amount to the “constitutionalization of the neoliberal nightmare.”
